text: Every gate you've learned so far has been described as a matrix acting on a state vector. Nobody who actually programs a quantum computer works that way day to day — they draw and read circuit diagrams, and this lesson teaches you that notation precisely enough to read someone else's circuit cold.

A circuit diagram has one wire per qubit, a timeline read left to right, left meaning earlier. A box on a wire is a single-qubit gate applied there. A controlled gate like CNOT is drawn as a filled dot on the control wire connected by a vertical line to a symbol, a circled plus, on the target wire — that vertical line just means these two marks happen together, as one operation. A measurement is a meter symbol, and after it the wire often becomes a double line, carrying a definite classical bit forward instead of quantum information.

Chapter 3's Bell-state circuit, drawn this way, shows an H box on qubit 1's wire followed by a control dot, connected down to an X symbol on qubit 2's wire at that same horizontal position. Reading it left to right recovers exactly the sequence already computed: H on qubit 1, then CNOT with qubit 1 as control and qubit 2 as target, starting from ket-00, giving ket-00 plus ket-11 over root 2. The diagram isn't a new object — it's the identical gate sequence in different notation.

Matrices are how you verify a circuit's behavior, but they don't scale as a way to author or read one — a 5-qubit circuit's full matrix is 32 by 32, and almost nobody writes that out. Diagrams scale the way source code does, one gate per line, however many qubits are involved. This is also exactly what real tools like Qiskit and Q#, covered in later courses in this catalog, render on screen: write circuit dot h of 0, then circuit dot c-x of 0 and 1, and the tool draws precisely this picture.
Next lesson defines two numbers that capture what a circuit actually costs to run on real hardware: its width and its depth.
